topics.name: Transcription
topics.kicker: Copying a gene’s DNA into RNA · Step one of making a protein
topics.dates: First step of gene expression: DNA → RNA → protein
topics.briefing: Transcription is how a cell copies a gene: an enzyme called RNA polymerase unzips a stretch of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA, using uracil wherever DNA would use thymine. In cells with a nucleus, like ours, it happens inside the nucleus, and the message gets edited before it leaves for a ribosome. It is the first arrow of Francis Crick’s “central dogma”: DNA makes RNA, and RNA makes protein.
topics.answerHtml: Transcription (accept RNA synthesis; prompt on gene expression; do not accept “translation” or “reverse transcription”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Roger Kornberg won the 2006 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for revealing how this process works in eukaryotes, 47 years after his father, Arthur, shared a Nobel Prize for work on how cells build DNA. In many eukaryotic genes, a short sequence called the TATA box helps mark where this process begins.
tossups.r: In this process, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads a gene and builds messenger RNA. For 10 points, name this first step of gene expression, in which DNA is copied into RNA.

tossups.p: In bacteria, a protein subunit called the sigma factor helps the enzyme that performs this process find a promoter sequence called the Pribnow box. Unlike DNA polymerase, that enzyme does not need a primer to start building its new strand.
tossups.r: That enzyme is RNA polymerase. For 10 points, name this process in which a cell copies a gene’s DNA into messenger RNA.

tossups.p: Alpha-amanitin, the main poison in the death cap mushroom, works by blocking one of the enzymes that perform this process in eukaryotes. Those cells use three main versions of that enzyme, numbered I, II, and III, and version II handles the genes that code for proteins.
tossups.r: In this process, RNA polymerase builds a strand of messenger RNA. For 10 points, name this process in which a gene’s DNA is copied into RNA.

tossups.p: Phillip Sharp and Richard Roberts shared a Nobel Prize for discovering that many genes copied in this process are “split” into pieces. In eukaryotes, the first product of this process is edited by a spliceosome, which cuts out introns and joins the exons together.
tossups.r: That product also gets a cap and a poly-A tail before it leaves the nucleus. For 10 points, name this process in which RNA polymerase copies DNA into messenger RNA.

tossups.p: Howard Temin and David Baltimore discovered an enzyme that lets retroviruses, such as HIV, run this process in reverse, building DNA from RNA. In the normal direction of this process, an enzyme reads only one DNA strand, called the template strand, and builds a matching strand.
tossups.r: Wherever the template has adenine, the new strand gets uracil. For 10 points, name this process that makes messenger RNA from DNA, the first step of gene expression.

tossups.p: In a bacterium’s lac operon, a repressor protein sits on a stretch of DNA called the operator, blocking this process until lactose is present. François Jacob and Jacques Monod [“moh-NOH”] proposed that model of gene control, which helped earn them a Nobel Prize.
tossups.r: This process starts when RNA polymerase binds to a promoter. For 10 points, name this process in which DNA is copied into messenger RNA.

tossups.p: In bacteria, this process can end when a protein called Rho catches up with the working enzyme, or when the new strand folds into a hairpin loop followed by a run of uracils. Those endings make up this process’s termination stage, which follows initiation and elongation.
tossups.r: In eukaryotes, it takes place in the nucleus. For 10 points, name this process in which RNA polymerase copies a gene’s DNA into RNA.

tossups.p: Sequences called enhancers, which can sit thousands of base pairs away from a gene, can boost how often that gene undergoes this process. In eukaryotes, helper proteins gather at a sequence called the TATA box to help start this process.
tossups.r: This process begins when RNA polymerase binds to a gene’s promoter. For 10 points, name this process that produces messenger RNA from a DNA template.

tossups.p: Bacteria use only one kind of enzyme to perform this process, pairing it with different sigma factors to read different sets of genes. Because bacteria lack a nucleus, their ribosomes can start translating a message while this process is still making it.
tossups.r: In eukaryotes, this process happens in the nucleus. For 10 points, name this first step of gene expression, in which RNA polymerase copies DNA into RNA.

tossups.p: Alternative splicing lets one gene produce several different proteins by joining the exons made in this process in different combinations. In eukaryotes, the product of this process is protected by a cap of modified guanine on one end and a long poly-A tail on the other.
tossups.r: This process uses uracil in place of thymine. For 10 points, name this process in which RNA polymerase copies DNA into messenger RNA.

tossups.p: Unlike DNA replication, which copies both strands of all of a cell’s DNA, this process copies only one strand of a gene, and its enzyme needs no primer to begin. The strand that gets read is called the template strand, while the other strand, the coding strand, matches the product except that it has thymine where the product has uracil.
tossups.r: This process is carried out by RNA polymerase. For 10 points, name this process that makes messenger RNA from DNA.

tossups.p: The antibiotic rifampin, used against tuberculosis, works by blocking the enzyme that performs this process in bacteria. In bacteria, that enzyme stops when its new strand folds into a hairpin loop or when a protein called Rho pulls it off the DNA.
tossups.r: In eukaryotic cells, this process happens in the nucleus. For 10 points, name this process in which RNA polymerase copies DNA into messenger RNA.

tossups.p: In bacteria, two short sequences found about 10 and 35 base pairs before a gene’s starting point, including one called the Pribnow box, signal where this process should begin. Those sequences are part of a region called the promoter.
tossups.r: In this process, RNA polymerase builds a strand of RNA that matches a gene. For 10 points, name this process that comes right before translation.

tossups.p: Walter Gilbert coined the terms “intron” and “exon” for the parts of a message that get cut out or kept after this process. Particles called snRNPs [“snurps”] combine into a spliceosome that does that cutting inside the nucleus.
tossups.r: Before that editing, RNA polymerase reads a DNA template to make the message. For 10 points, name this process in which a gene is copied into RNA.

tossups.p: In the nucleolus, an enzyme numbered I carries out this process to make most of the RNA found in ribosomes, while a related enzyme numbered III makes transfer RNA. In every version of this process, the new strand grows in the five-prime to three-prime direction.
tossups.r: In eukaryotes, this process occurs in the nucleus, where RNA polymerase reads a gene. For 10 points, name this first step of gene expression, which copies DNA into RNA.

clues.t: A cell copies a gene’s DNA into a matching strand of RNA, usually messenger RNA (mRNA)
First step of gene expression; the next step, translation, reads the mRNA at a ribosome to build a protein
In eukaryotes (cells with a nucleus), it happens inside the nucleus
The first arrow of Francis Crick’s “central dogma”: DNA → RNA → protein
Carried out by the enzyme RNA polymerase, which reads one strand of DNA
RNA polymerase starts at a DNA region called the promoter, just before a gene
Many eukaryotic promoters contain the TATA box, a short sequence rich in thymine and adenine
The new RNA gets uracil (U) wherever DNA would have thymine (T), so adenine pairs with uracil
Only the template (antisense) strand is read; the other, coding (sense) strand matches the mRNA, but with T instead of U
Three stages: initiation, elongation, and termination
The template is read 3′ to 5′, so the new RNA grows in the 5′ to 3′ direction
In eukaryotes the pre-mRNA is spliced: noncoding introns are cut out and the exons are joined
Eukaryotic mRNA also gets a 5′ cap and a poly-A tail before leaving the nucleus
Bacteria have no nucleus, so it happens in the cytoplasm, and ribosomes can start translating before it ends
In bacteria, a sigma factor helps RNA polymerase recognize the promoter; bacteria have just one kind of RNA polymerase
Bacterial promoters have a −10 sequence (the Pribnow box, TATAAT) and a −35 sequence
Bacteria end it with the Rho protein or with a hairpin loop in the RNA followed by a run of U’s
Unlike DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase needs no primer to start a new strand
Eukaryotes use three main RNA polymerases: I makes most ribosomal RNA (in the nucleolus), II makes mRNA, and III makes transfer RNA
RNA polymerase II cannot find a promoter on its own; helper proteins must first gather at the TATA box
Enhancers, DNA sequences that can sit thousands of base pairs away, can boost how often a gene is copied
Introns are cut out by the spliceosome, built from snRNPs (“snurps”); alternative splicing lets one gene make several proteins
Phillip Sharp and Richard Roberts discovered “split genes” and shared the 1993 Nobel Prize; Walter Gilbert named introns and exons
Alpha-amanitin, the main toxin of the death cap mushroom, blocks RNA polymerase II
The tuberculosis antibiotic rifampin blocks bacterial RNA polymerase
Roger Kornberg won the 2006 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying it in eukaryotes; his father, Arthur, shared the 1959 Nobel for work on making DNA
Retroviruses like HIV run it backward, copying RNA into DNA; Howard Temin and David Baltimore found the enzyme that does this (1970)
In the lac operon, a repressor sits on the operator and blocks it until lactose is present (Jacob and Monod’s model)

trap.title: Transcription or translation?
trap.body: The two steps of gene expression sound alike and happen one right after the other. Transcription copies DNA into messenger RNA, inside the nucleus; translation then reads that messenger RNA at a ribosome to build a protein. Players also confuse it with DNA replication, which copies all of a cell’s DNA before the cell divides, and with reverse transcription, which HIV uses to turn RNA into DNA.
trap.fix: Listen for the product. RNA polymerase, promoters, the TATA box, uracil replacing thymine, or introns being spliced out mean transcription. Ribosomes, codons, tRNA, or amino acids being linked mean translation. Helicase, primers, Okazaki fragments, or DNA polymerase mean replication.
trap.line: Real answer line: Transcription (prompt on gene expression; do not accept “translation” or “reverse transcription”)

topics.name: Tundra
topics.kicker: Cold, treeless biome of the far north · Frozen permafrost underneath
topics.dates: Growing season of only about two months
topics.briefing: The tundra is the coldest biome on Earth: a treeless land in the far north, and on high mountaintops, where winters are long and dark and summer lasts only a couple of months. Just under the surface lies permafrost, ground that stays frozen all year, so trees cannot put down deep roots. Instead, mosses, lichens, and low shrubs feed caribou, musk oxen, and lemmings, while arctic foxes and snowy owls hunt.
topics.answerHtml: Tundra (accept Arctic tundra or alpine tundra; prompt on Arctic or alpine; do not accept “taiga” or “permafrost”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the Köppen climate system, this biome’s climate is labeled ET, which means its warmest month averages between 0 and 10 degrees Celsius. Each summer, only a thin top layer of soil in this biome, called the active layer, thaws out.
tossups.r: Below that layer lies permafrost. For 10 points, name this cold, treeless biome found north of the taiga.

tossups.p: Antarctic hair grass and Antarctic pearlwort, the only native flowering plants in Antarctica, grow in a southern version of this biome. A mountain version of this biome is found above the tree line, where pikas and marmots live.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cold, treeless biome whose Arctic version has permanently frozen ground called permafrost and is home to caribou.

tossups.p: Musk oxen in this biome grow a soft underwool called qiviut [“KIV-ee-ut”], and when wolves attack, the adults form a circle around their calves. Caribou in this biome dig through the snow to eat “reindeer moss,” which is actually a lichen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this treeless Arctic biome where the ground below the surface, called permafrost, stays frozen all year.

tossups.p: Hills called pingos [“PING-gohz”] form in this biome when a growing core of ice pushes the ground upward. Freezing and thawing also crack the ground in this biome into polygon-shaped patterns that can be seen from the air.
tossups.r: Those features form in its permafrost. For 10 points, name this cold, treeless biome found across northern Alaska, Canada, and Siberia.

tossups.p: The cup-shaped flowers of this biome’s Arctic poppy turn to follow the sun, warming the insects that crawl inside them. Plants in this biome grow low to the ground and bloom quickly, because its growing season lasts only about two months.
tossups.r: Mosses, lichens, and dwarf shrubs grow in this biome, which has no trees. For 10 points, name this cold biome of the far north.

tossups.p: Arctic ground squirrels in this biome survive the winter by hibernating with body temperatures that drop below freezing. Under the snow, lemmings in this biome stay busy all winter in tunnels in a layer called the subnivean [“sub-NIV-ee-un”] zone.
tossups.r: Snowy owls and arctic foxes hunt those lemmings. For 10 points, name this treeless biome of the far north, where the ground stays frozen as permafrost.

tossups.p: The Porcupine caribou herd migrates each spring to give birth on the coastal plain of Alaska’s Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, which lies in this biome. Swarms of mosquitoes fill this biome in summer, when melted snow collects in bogs and ponds.
tossups.r: Caribou, musk oxen, and lemmings live in this biome. For 10 points, name this cold, treeless biome found north of the taiga.

tossups.p: Nenets [“NEN-ets”] herders in Siberia lead their reindeer across this biome on long yearly migrations, and Sami people in northern Scandinavia also herd reindeer here. In summer, the sun here can stay up all night, but the growing season lasts only about two months.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cold, treeless biome, home to musk oxen and lemmings, that lies north of the boreal forest.

tossups.p: The willow ptarmigan [“TAR-mih-gun”], Alaska’s state bird, lives in this biome and grows feathers on its feet that work like snowshoes. Arctic foxes in this biome turn white in winter and have small ears that lose less body heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cold, treeless biome of the far north, where caribou graze on lichens above frozen permafrost.

tossups.p: Populations of lemmings in this biome boom and crash every few years, and the numbers of snowy owls and arctic foxes that eat them rise and fall along with them. Food webs in this biome are simple because few species can survive its long, dark winters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cold, treeless biome found north of the taiga, where permafrost lies under the soil.

tossups.p: Norway built its Global Seed Vault inside a mountain on Svalbard, an Arctic island chain where this biome is found, partly because the frozen rock would keep the seeds cold even without power. This biome gets so little rain and snow that it is sometimes compared to a desert.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this treeless biome of the far north, where the frozen ground is called permafrost.

tossups.p: American pikas living in a mountain version of this biome gather grasses and flowers into “haypiles” to eat during the winter, since they do not hibernate. That mountain version is found above the tree line, the elevation where trees stop growing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cold, treeless biome whose Arctic version covers much of northern Canada and Siberia.

tossups.p: The Arctic willow, one of the northernmost woody plants on Earth, creeps flat along the ground in this biome instead of growing tall. Cushion plants such as moss campion also grow in this biome in low, rounded mounds that stay out of the drying wind.
tossups.r: Lichens and mosses cover much of this biome, which has no trees. For 10 points, name this cold biome of the far north, underlain by permafrost.

tossups.p: Lemmings in this biome stay active all winter in tunnels beneath the snow, in a layer called the subnivean [“sub-NIV-ee-un”] zone, where the snow traps warmth like a blanket. Arctic foxes in this biome can hear those lemmings moving under the snow and pounce down on them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cold, treeless biome where permafrost lies beneath the soil and caribou graze on lichens.

tossups.p: Thermokarst lakes and pits form in this biome when its ice-rich ground melts and the land slumps. Scientists worry that as this biome warms, microbes will break down the carbon stored in its soils and release carbon dioxide and methane.
tossups.r: That ice-rich ground is called permafrost. For 10 points, name this treeless biome of the far north, home to caribou and arctic foxes.

clues.t: A cold, treeless biome of the far north; it is the coldest biome on Earth
Underlain by permafrost, a layer of ground that stays frozen all year
Its plants are short: mosses, lichens, sedges, grasses, and dwarf shrubs
Home to caribou (reindeer), musk oxen, arctic foxes, lemmings, and snowy owls
Lies north of the taiga (boreal forest), beyond the tree line where trees stop growing
An alpine version lies above the tree line on high mountains, where pikas gather “haypiles” of plants for winter and marmots hibernate
Growing season of only about two months; under the summer “midnight sun,” it can stay light all night
Gets very little precipitation, often less than 25 centimeters (10 inches) a year, so it is compared to a desert
Only the top layer of soil, called the active layer, thaws each summer
Meltwater cannot soak into the frozen ground, so summer brings bogs, ponds, and swarms of mosquitoes
Caribou dig through snow to eat “reindeer moss,” which is really a lichen
Arctic foxes turn white in winter and have small ears that lose less heat; they pounce on lemmings they hear under the snow
Its frozen soils store huge amounts of carbon; as they thaw, microbes release carbon dioxide and methane, adding to climate change
Low biodiversity and simple food webs, since few species survive its long, dark winters
Köppen climate code ET: the warmest month averages between 0 °C and 10 °C
Antarctica’s only two native flowering plants, Antarctic hair grass and Antarctic pearlwort, grow in its Antarctic version
Musk oxen grow a soft underwool called qiviut and form a defensive circle around their calves when wolves attack
Pingos are hills pushed up by a growing core of ice; freezing and thawing crack the ground into polygon patterns
Thermokarst lakes and pits form where ice-rich frozen ground melts and the land slumps
Arctic poppy flowers turn to follow the sun, warming the insects that crawl inside them
Plants hug the ground: the Arctic willow creeps along the soil, and cushion plants like moss campion grow in low mounds
Arctic ground squirrels hibernate with body temperatures that drop below freezing
Lemmings stay active all winter in tunnels under the snow, in the subnivean zone
Lemming populations boom and crash every few years, and snowy owl and arctic fox numbers rise and fall with them
The willow ptarmigan, Alaska’s state bird, has feathered feet that work like snowshoes
The Porcupine caribou herd gives birth on the coastal plain of Alaska’s Arctic National Wildlife Refuge
Sami people in northern Scandinavia and Nenets people in Siberia herd reindeer across it
Norway’s Global Seed Vault was dug into a mountain on Arctic Svalbard, where frozen rock keeps the seeds cold even without power

trap.title: Tundra, not taiga
trap.body: The tundra and the taiga sit side by side across Alaska, Canada, Scandinavia, and Siberia, and both have long, cold winters, so players mix them up. The taiga (boreal forest) is the huge belt of evergreen forest to the south; the tundra begins where those trees stop, at the tree line. Permafrost is a second trap: it is the frozen ground under the tundra, not the biome itself.
trap.fix: Spruce, fir, pine, moose, or lynx point to the taiga. No trees, lichens, musk oxen, lemmings, or pingos point to the tundra. A mountaintop above the tree line is still the tundra (alpine tundra).
trap.line: Real answer line: Tundra (accept Arctic tundra or alpine tundra; do not accept “taiga” or “permafrost”)

topics.name: Alzheimer’s disease
topics.kicker: Most common cause of dementia · Plaques and tangles in the brain
topics.briefing: Alzheimer’s disease is a brain disease that slowly harms memory and thinking, and it is the most common cause of dementia in older adults. It is named for Alois Alzheimer, a German doctor who in 1906 described two kinds of damage in a patient’s brain: clumps of protein called amyloid plaques and twisted fibers called tangles. There is no cure yet, but scientists keep testing new medicines, including ones that clear away the plaques.
topics.answerHtml: Alzheimer’s disease (accept AD; prompt on dementia; do not accept “Parkinson’s disease”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Emil Kraepelin gave this disease its name in a 1910 psychiatry textbook, honoring a colleague who had described it four years earlier. That colleague had found clumps of protein called plaques and twisted fibers called tangles while studying a patient’s brain under a microscope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease named for a German doctor, the most common cause of dementia.

tossups.p: This disease was first described in Auguste Deter [“ow-GOOS-tuh DAY-ter”], a woman in her fifties who was treated at a hospital in Frankfurt, Germany. After her death in 1906, her doctor studied her brain under a microscope and found unusual clumps and tangles.
tossups.r: That doctor gave his name to this disease. For 10 points, name this brain disease that causes memory loss and is the most common cause of dementia.

tossups.p: Brain scans of people with this disease show the brain’s outer layer, the cortex, shrinking over time, while fluid-filled spaces called ventricles grow larger. Twisted fibers called neurofibrillary tangles, made of a protein called tau [“TOW”], build up inside neurons in this disease.
tossups.r: Clumps of beta-amyloid also build up between neurons in this disease. For 10 points, name this brain disease, the most common cause of dementia.

tossups.p: People who inherit two copies of the APOE4 version of a gene on chromosome 19 have a much higher risk of the common, late-onset form of this disease. The protein made by that gene helps carry fats such as cholesterol through the blood and brain.
tossups.r: In this disease, plaques of beta-amyloid protein build up in the brain. For 10 points, name this most common cause of dementia in older adults.

tossups.p: Rare inherited forms of this disease, which can begin when people are in their 30s to 50s, are often caused by mutations in the presenilin genes. Enzymes called secretases cut a larger protein into the beta-amyloid pieces that build up in this disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this brain disease marked by amyloid plaques and tau tangles, the most common cause of dementia.

tossups.p: John Hardy and Gerald Higgins named the amyloid cascade hypothesis, which says that a buildup of one protein fragment sets off the other damage seen in this disease. Clumps of that fragment, beta-amyloid, form sticky plaques between neurons in people with this disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that slowly destroys memory, the most common cause of dementia in older adults.

tossups.p: In healthy neurons, the protein tau helps hold microtubules steady, like ties on a railroad track, but in this disease tau twists into tangles inside the cells. The damage in this disease usually begins in and around the hippocampus.
tossups.r: That brain region helps form new memories. For 10 points, name this brain disease, the most common cause of dementia, that is also marked by amyloid plaques.

tossups.p: In 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration gave full approval to lecanemab [“leh-KAN-eh-mab”], an antibody drug that removes beta-amyloid from the brain and modestly slows the early stages of this disease. Older drugs for this disease, such as donepezil [“doh-NEP-eh-zil”], keep more of the chemical messenger acetylcholine available in the brain.
tossups.r: This disease leaves amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the brain. For 10 points, name this disease, the most common cause of dementia.

tossups.p: Special dyes let PET scans show beta-amyloid plaques in the living brains of people with this disease. Before such scans existed, doctors could confirm this disease for certain only by studying brain tissue after a person had died.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this brain disease that destroys memory, the most common cause of dementia in older adults.

tossups.p: David Snowdon’s Nun Study followed School Sisters of Notre Dame for years and found that nuns whose early-life writing was packed with ideas were less likely to develop this disease. Some of those nuns stayed sharp even though their brains showed this disease’s plaques and tangles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most common cause of dementia, a disease that slowly destroys memory.

tossups.p: In Lisa Genova’s novel _Still Alice_, a Harvard professor learns that she has an early-onset form of this disease. Julianne Moore won the Academy Award for Best Actress for playing that professor in the 2014 film version.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this brain disease that causes memory loss and is the most common cause of dementia.

tossups.p: Tennessee women’s basketball coach Pat Summitt and country singer Glen Campbell both spoke publicly about living with this disease after their diagnoses in 2011. Campbell’s song “I’m Not Gonna Miss You,” about his illness, won a Grammy Award.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that slowly destroys memory, the most common cause of dementia.

tossups.p: Because the gene for amyloid precursor protein sits on chromosome 21, people with Down syndrome, who have an extra copy of that chromosome, have a higher risk of this disease. In this disease, pieces of that protein, called beta-amyloid, clump into plaques.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this brain disease that causes memory loss, the most common cause of dementia.

tossups.p: The drug memantine [“MEM-an-teen”] treats this disease by blocking a receptor for the chemical messenger glutamate. Neurons that make another messenger, acetylcholine, die early in this disease, so drugs such as donepezil slow acetylcholine’s breakdown.
tossups.r: People with this disease develop amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the brain. For 10 points, name this most common cause of dementia.

tossups.p: In 1983, a U.S. president named November a national awareness month for this disease. Eleven years later, in a handwritten letter, that same president announced that he had this disease and wrote that he was beginning “the journey that will lead me into the sunset of my life.”
tossups.r: That president was Ronald Reagan. For 10 points, name this brain disease that causes memory loss, the most common cause of dementia.

clues.t: The most common cause of dementia, a loss of memory and thinking skills serious enough to affect daily life
A brain illness that gets worse over time, first harming memory of recent events and later other thinking skills
Named for a German psychiatrist and brain scientist who described it in 1906
Most people who have it are over 65, and there is no cure yet
Clumps of a protein fragment called beta-amyloid form amyloid plaques between neurons
Twisted fibers of a protein called tau form neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons
Neurodegenerative: neurons stop working and die, and the brain shrinks over time
Damage usually starts in and around the hippocampus, the brain region that helps form new memories

Neurons that make acetylcholine die early; drugs like donepezil slow acetylcholine’s breakdown
Most cases begin after age 65; early-onset cases start younger, and some rare forms are inherited
People with Down syndrome have a higher risk, because chromosome 21 carries the gene for amyloid precursor protein
Emil Kraepelin gave it its name in a 1910 psychiatry textbook, honoring his colleague
First described in Auguste Deter, a woman in her fifties treated in Frankfurt; her brain was studied after her death in 1906
Brain scans show the cortex shrinking and the fluid-filled ventricles growing larger as the illness gets worse
Two copies of APOE4, a version of a gene on chromosome 19 whose protein carries cholesterol, greatly raise the risk of the late-onset form
Mutations in the presenilin genes cause rare inherited early-onset forms; secretase enzymes cut a larger protein into beta-amyloid
John Hardy and Gerald Higgins’s amyloid cascade hypothesis (1992) says beta-amyloid buildup sets off the rest of the damage
Tau normally holds microtubules steady inside neurons, like ties on a railroad track
In 2023, the FDA gave full approval to lecanemab, an antibody drug that clears beta-amyloid and modestly slows the early stages
PET scans with special dyes can show amyloid plaques in a living brain; before that, it was confirmed only after death
David Snowdon’s Nun Study of the School Sisters of Notre Dame linked idea-packed early writing to a lower risk
Lisa Genova’s novel _Still Alice_ follows a Harvard professor with an early-onset form; Julianne Moore won an Oscar in the 2014 film
Coach Pat Summitt and singer Glen Campbell spoke publicly about their 2011 diagnoses; Campbell’s “I’m Not Gonna Miss You” won a Grammy
The drug memantine blocks a receptor for the chemical messenger glutamate

trap.title: Not just “dementia”
trap.body: Dementia is a general word for a decline in memory and thinking, and Alzheimer’s disease is only its most common cause, so saying “dementia” earns a prompt, not points. Parkinson’s disease is the other trap: it is also a brain disease that is more common in older adults, but it mainly affects movement and involves the loss of neurons that make dopamine.
trap.fix: Amyloid plaques, tau tangles, the hippocampus, acetylcholine drugs, and a German doctor in 1906 mean Alzheimer’s. Tremors, dopamine, Lewy bodies, and the substantia nigra mean Parkinson’s. If the question itself says “dementia,” the answer is the disease that causes it.
trap.line: Real answer line: Alzheimer’s disease (accept AD; prompt on dementia)

topics.name: Apoptosis
topics.kicker: Programmed cell death · Cells take themselves apart neatly
topics.briefing: Apoptosis is programmed cell death: a tidy, step-by-step way for a cell to take itself apart when it is damaged or no longer needed. Before you were born, it carved your fingers apart by removing the webbing between them. Enzymes called caspases chop the cell up from the inside, and white blood cells eat the leftover pieces, so nothing spills out to cause inflammation.
topics.answerHtml: Apoptosis (accept programmed cell death; prompt on cell death; do not accept “necrosis” or “autophagy”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the hermaphrodite form of the worm _Caenorhabditis elegans_ [“SEE-noh-rab-DY-tiss EL-uh-ganz”], exactly 131 of the 1,090 body cells formed during development die by this process. H. Robert Horvitz, John Sulston, and Sydney Brenner shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine partly for studying this process in that worm.
tossups.r: This process is carried out by enzymes called caspases. For 10 points, name this orderly form of cell death, which removes the webbing between a developing embryo’s fingers.

tossups.p: Many of the extra neurons made in a developing nervous system die by this process, especially ones that fail to connect to a target. Ducks keep their webbed feet because a protein blocks the signal for this process between their toes, while in chickens this process removes that webbing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tidy form of cell death, a cell’s planned self-destruction, which, unlike necrosis, causes no inflammation.

tossups.p: John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie [“WY-lee”], and Alastair Currie named this process in 1972, choosing a Greek word that describes leaves falling off a tree. During this process, the cell shrinks and breaks into small membrane-wrapped packets.
tossups.r: Macrophages eat those packets, so nothing spills out to cause inflammation. For 10 points, name this orderly form of cell death.

tossups.p: When cytochrome c leaks out of the mitochondria, it binds a protein called Apaf-1, forming a wheel-shaped complex that switches on caspase-9 and starts the intrinsic pathway of this process. That pathway is often triggered when a cell’s DNA is badly damaged.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this form of cell death in which a cell neatly takes itself apart, as when it removes the webbing between an embryo’s fingers and toes.

tossups.p: A protein called Fas ligand binds to a “death receptor” called Fas to start the extrinsic pathway of this process, which switches on caspase-8. That initiator caspase then turns on executioner caspases, such as caspase-3, that chop apart the cell’s proteins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, a cell’s orderly self-destruction, which is different from messy necrosis.

tossups.p: Radiation and many chemotherapy drugs fight cancer partly by damaging cancer cells’ DNA so badly that the cells undergo this process. Cancer cells often avoid this process, which lets damaged cells keep dividing.
tossups.r: This process is carried out by enzymes called caspases. For 10 points, name this tidy form of cell death that removes damaged or unneeded cells.

tossups.p: Douglas Hanahan and Robert Weinberg listed “evading” this process as one of the hallmarks of cancer. The protein p53, nicknamed the “guardian of the genome,” can trigger this process when a cell’s DNA is too damaged to repair.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this form of cell death, carried out by enzymes called caspases, in which a cell destroys itself in an orderly way.

tossups.p: During this process, a lipid called phosphatidylserine [“foss-fuh-TY-dul-SAIR-een”] flips from the inner to the outer side of the cell membrane, where it acts as an “eat me” signal. Macrophages that sense that signal swallow the cell’s remains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this orderly form of cell death that, unlike necrosis, does not cause inflammation.

tossups.p: Enzymes chop a cell’s DNA into regular-sized pieces during this process, so the DNA forms a “ladder” pattern when it is run on a gel. During this process, the cell’s membrane bulges out in bubbles called blebs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tidy form of cell death, which removes the webbing between a developing embryo’s fingers.

tossups.p: Cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells trigger this process in infected cells by releasing perforin, which opens pores in the target cell, and granzymes, which enter through those pores. Inside the target cell, enzymes called caspases then carry out this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, a cell’s orderly self-destruction, which is different from necrosis.

tossups.p: In the thymus, young T cells that would attack the body’s own tissues are removed by this process during negative selection. This process also removes a tadpole’s tail during metamorphosis, a change triggered by thyroid hormone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this orderly form of cell death, in which caspases help a cell take itself apart.

tossups.p: Skin cells badly damaged by the ultraviolet light in sunlight destroy themselves by this process, and scientists call those dying cells “sunburn cells.” During this process, the cell shrinks and its chromatin clumps together.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tidy form of cell death that removes unneeded cells, like the webbing between an embryo’s fingers.

tossups.p: Some viruses carry genes that block this process, keeping the cells they infect alive long enough to make many new copies of the virus. Release of cytochrome c from mitochondria starts this process’s intrinsic pathway.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this orderly form of cell death that, unlike necrosis, causes no inflammation.

tossups.p: Caspase-3 and caspase-7 act as “executioner” enzymes in this process, cutting apart key proteins inside the cell. One of those cuts frees an enzyme that chops the cell’s DNA into pieces, and the cell then splits into small packets that neighboring cells can eat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this form of cell death, in which a cell neatly takes itself apart instead of bursting as in necrosis.

tossups.p: Neutrophils, short-lived white blood cells, normally die by this process after an infection has been cleared, and macrophages then eat them. During this process, a cell shrinks and breaks into small membrane-wrapped packets instead of bursting open.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this orderly self-destruction of cells, which removes the webbing between an embryo’s fingers and toes.

Removes the webbing between the fingers and toes of a developing embryo
Unlike necrosis (messy cell death from injury, where cells swell and burst), it is tidy and causes no inflammation
Removes damaged, infected, or unneeded cells for the good of the whole body

Carried out by protein-cutting enzymes called caspases
The cell shrinks, its membrane bulges out in blebs, and it breaks into small membrane-wrapped packets

Named in 1972 by John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie, and Alastair Currie
In the worm C. elegans, exactly 131 of the 1,090 body cells made in a hermaphrodite die this way
Sydney Brenner, H. Robert Horvitz, and John Sulston shared the 2002 Nobel Prize partly for studying it in the worm C. elegans
Many extra neurons made in a developing nervous system die this way, especially ones that fail to connect to a target

Its DNA is chopped into regular-sized pieces that form a “ladder” pattern on a gel

trap.title: Apoptosis, not necrosis
trap.body: Both are ways a cell dies, so players who hear “cell death” buzz with the first one they think of. Necrosis is messy, accidental death from injury or loss of blood flow: the cell swells and bursts, and its leaking contents cause inflammation. Autophagy, in which a cell digests some of its own parts inside lysosomes, is a second trap; it often helps a cell survive.
trap.fix: Planned, tidy, shrinking, caspases, cytochrome c, blebs, and webbing between fingers mean apoptosis. Swelling, bursting, injury, and inflammation mean necrosis. “Self-eating” and lysosomes mean autophagy.
trap.line: Real answer line: Apoptosis (accept programmed cell death; prompt on cell death; do not accept “necrosis”)

topics.name: Cellulose
topics.kicker: Glucose chains in plant cell walls · Most abundant organic compound
topics.briefing: Cellulose is the tough material that gives plants their strength: long chains of thousands of glucose units, bundled into fibers that build plant cell walls. It is the most abundant organic compound on Earth and makes up most of cotton and paper and much of wood. Humans cannot digest it, so it passes through us as fiber, but cows and termites rely on tiny microbes in their guts to break it down.
topics.answerHtml: Cellulose (prompt on fiber or polysaccharide; do not accept “cellulase,” “starch,” or “chitin”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: French chemist Anselme Payen [“pah-YAN”] isolated this substance from plant material in 1838 and worked out its chemical formula. Unlike starch, which is built from the same sugar, this substance cannot be broken down by the enzymes in the human gut.
tossups.r: So it passes through the body as dietary fiber. For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that forms plant cell walls.

tossups.p: Christian Schönbein [“SHURN-bine”] invented an explosive called guncotton by treating this substance with nitric acid. Other chemical treatments turn this substance into fabrics such as rayon, which was first sold as “artificial silk.”
tossups.r: Cotton is mostly made of this substance. For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that builds plant cell walls.

tossups.p: John Wesley Hyatt mixed a nitric acid–treated form of this substance with camphor to make an early plastic meant to replace ivory in billiard balls. That plastic was later used for photographic film and movie film.
tossups.r: This substance itself is a chain of glucose units that forms plant cell walls. For 10 points, name this most abundant organic compound on Earth.

tossups.p: Tunicates, such as sea squirts, are the only animals known to make this substance, which forms their tough outer coat, or tunic. Animals such as cows and termites can digest this substance only with help from microbes living in their guts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this polysaccharide, made of glucose, that forms the cell walls of plants.

tossups.p: Water molds, or oomycetes [“oh-uh-MY-seets”], have cell walls made of this substance instead of chitin, which is one way to tell them apart from true fungi. In plants, chains of this substance bundle into strands called microfibrils.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this glucose polymer that makes up most of the cell walls of plants.

tossups.p: In plants, rosette-shaped enzyme complexes sitting in the cell membrane spin out long chains of this substance, which bundle into microfibrils held together by hydrogen bonds. Each glucose unit in this substance’s chains is flipped relative to its neighbors, keeping the chains straight.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that is the main component of plant cell walls.

tossups.p: The rubbery mat that forms on top of kombucha and the chewy dessert nata de coco are both made of a pure form of this substance produced by bacteria. Unlike starch, this substance links its glucose units with beta-1,4 bonds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that forms plant cell walls and that humans cannot digest.

tossups.p: Many termites depend on protists in their guts, such as _Trichonympha_ [“trik-oh-NIM-fuh”], to break down this substance in the wood they eat. Cows also rely on microbes, which ferment this substance in the rumen, the first chamber of a cow’s stomach.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that forms plant cell walls and passes through humans as dietary fiber.

tossups.p: In the viscose process, chemicals turn this substance into a thick liquid that is squeezed through tiny holes into an acid bath, forming threads of the fabric rayon. Because hydrogen bonds pack its chains tightly together, this substance does not dissolve in water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that makes up plant cell walls, cotton, and paper.

tossups.p: Horses and rabbits ferment this substance in an enlarged pouch called the cecum [“SEE-kum”], where gut microbes break it down. Iodine turns starch blue-black, but it does not stain this other chain of glucose the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this polysaccharide, the main building material of plant cell walls.

tossups.p: Unlike the coiled chains of starch, which use alpha bonds, the glucose units in this substance are linked by beta-1,4 glycosidic [“gly-koh-SID-ik”] bonds into long, straight chains. In wood, fibers of this substance are glued together by a tough polymer called lignin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most abundant organic compound on Earth, which forms plant cell walls.

tossups.p: In the kraft process, wood chips are cooked with sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide to dissolve the lignin and free this substance’s fibers. Every other glucose unit in a chain of this substance is flipped upside down, so the chains stay straight.
tossups.r: This substance is the main ingredient of paper. For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that forms plant cell walls.

tossups.p: Count Hilaire de Chardonnet [“shar-doh-NAY”] made an “artificial silk” from this substance in the 1880s. Inside a cow’s rumen, the first chamber of its stomach, microbes ferment this substance, and chewing cud helps break it down further.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that forms plant cell walls and makes up most of cotton.

tossups.p: Food companies add a powdered form of this substance to shredded cheese to keep the shreds from clumping together. This substance is also the largest single part of wood, where its fibers are bound together by lignin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that is the main part of plant cell walls, cotton, and paper.

tossups.p: Chitin, found in insect exoskeletons, has nearly the same structure as this substance, except that each of chitin’s sugars carries a nitrogen-containing group. Both chitin and this substance are tough building materials made of long chains of sugars.
tossups.r: This substance passes through the human body as dietary fiber. For 10 points, name this polysaccharide that builds plant cell walls.

A polysaccharide: a long, unbranched chain of thousands of glucose units
The most abundant organic compound on Earth
Humans cannot digest it, so it passes through the body as dietary fiber (roughage)
Cotton is about 90 percent this substance, and it is the main ingredient of paper
Its glucose units are joined by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds; starch uses alpha bonds instead
Every other glucose unit in the chain is flipped upside down, so the chain stays straight

Cows, termites, and other plant-eaters digest it only with help from microbes living in their guts

In wood, its fibers are glued together by a tough polymer called lignin
Treated with chemicals, it can be turned into rayon fabric and clear cellophane wrap
Plants store glucose as starch but build with this; iodine turns starch blue-black but not this
Fungi and insects build with chitin, a similar chain whose sugars carry a nitrogen-containing group
French chemist Anselme Payen isolated it from plant material in 1838
Christian Schönbein made the explosive guncotton by treating it with nitric acid
John Wesley Hyatt mixed a nitrated form with camphor to make an early plastic for billiard balls, later used for film

trap.title: Cellulose, not cellulase
trap.body: Cellulose is the fiber itself, while cellulase (ending in “-ase,” like most enzymes) is the enzyme that breaks it down, and a one-letter slip changes the answer. Starch and glycogen are the other traps: they are also chains of glucose, but they are energy stores that our bodies can digest, while cellulose is a building material we cannot digest. Chitin is the look-alike building material of fungi and insect shells.
trap.fix: Plant cell walls, fiber, cotton, paper, wood, termites, and beta bonds mean cellulose. Food storage in potatoes and seeds means starch; storage in liver and muscle means glycogen; exoskeletons and mushrooms mean chitin. Spell and say it with “-ose,” the ending for sugars.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cellulose (prompt on fiber or polysaccharide; do not accept “cellulase”)

topics.name: Cystic fibrosis
topics.kicker: Inherited disease of thick, sticky mucus · Caused by the CFTR gene
topics.briefing: Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disease that makes the body’s mucus thick and sticky, which can clog the lungs and the pancreas. It comes from changes in one gene, CFTR, which normally builds a channel that moves chloride, part of salt, across cell membranes; that is why people with it have extra-salty sweat. A child has it only after inheriting a changed copy from each parent, and new medicines have greatly helped many people with it.
topics.answerHtml: Cystic fibrosis (accept CF or mucoviscidosis; prompt on fibrosis; do not accept “pulmonary fibrosis”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1938, pathologist Dorothy Hansine Andersen named this disease after the fluid-filled sacs and scar tissue she found in the pancreas of young children. Mucus can block the pancreas in this disease, so many people with it take enzyme capsules with meals to help digest their food.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited disease, caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, that makes mucus thick and sticky.

tossups.p: In 1989, Lap-Chee Tsui [“LAP-chee CHOY”], Francis Collins, and John Riordan identified the gene behind this disease on chromosome 7. That gene codes for a channel protein that moves chloride ions out of the cells lining the lungs and gut.
tossups.r: That gene is CFTR. For 10 points, name this genetic disease that causes thick, sticky mucus and very salty sweat.

tossups.p: The most common mutation behind this disease, called F508del or delta F508, deletes three DNA bases and removes a single phenylalanine from a protein. Without that amino acid, the protein folds the wrong way, so the cell destroys it before it can reach the cell membrane.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited disease, caused by changes in the CFTR gene, that clogs the lungs with thick mucus.

tossups.p: In 2019, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Trikafta, a combination of elexacaftor, tezacaftor, and ivacaftor that helps a faulty channel protein fold correctly and stay open in people with this disease. That channel normally carries chloride ions out of cells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this genetic disease that makes the mucus in the lungs thick and sticky.

tossups.p: Ivacaftor, sold as Kalydeco, became the first drug aimed at the root cause of this disease when it was approved in 2012 for people with a mutation called G551D. Before such drugs, care for this disease focused on clearing mucus and fighting lung infections.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited disease that people get by receiving two faulty copies of the CFTR gene.

tossups.p: During a 1948 New York heat wave, Paul di Sant’Agnese [“dee sahnt-ah-NYAY-zay”] noticed that children with this disease were especially likely to get sick from the heat, which led him to discover that their sweat holds extra salt. That discovery led to the sweat test used to diagnose this disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this genetic disease, caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, that leaves thick, sticky mucus in the lungs.

tossups.p: In 1959, Lewis Gibson and Robert Cooke developed a standard test for this disease that uses the drug pilocarpine [“py-loh-KAR-peen”] and a weak electric current to make a small patch of skin sweat. That test measures how much chloride is in the sweat.
tossups.r: People with this disease have unusually salty sweat. For 10 points, name this genetic disease that makes mucus thick and sticky.

tossups.p: In 1965, a four-year-old boy named Richard Weiss told his mother he knew she was working to help children with “sixty-five roses,” his way of saying this disease’s name. Roses then became a symbol of a foundation that raises money for research on this disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited disease, caused by the CFTR gene, that makes mucus thick and sticky.

tossups.p: The title of the 2019 film _Five Feet Apart_ plays on a rule that people with this disease should stay at least six feet away from each other, so that they do not pass harmful bacteria back and forth. One such germ, _Pseudomonas aeruginosa_ [“soo-doh-MOH-nuss air-oo-jih-NOH-suh”], often infects the lungs of people with this disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this genetic disease, caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, that clogs the lungs with thick, sticky mucus.

tossups.p: Many people with this disease breathe in dornase alfa, an enzyme that thins mucus by cutting apart DNA left behind by white blood cells. They also loosen mucus every day with airway-clearance routines, such as wearing a vest that shakes the chest.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this inherited disease, caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, that makes mucus thick and sticky.

tossups.p: Some scientists have proposed that carriers of this disease’s gene were better protected against cholera, because cholera’s toxin makes that gene’s chloride channels pour salt and water into the gut. Carriers have one changed copy of the gene and usually have no symptoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this recessive genetic disease, in which two faulty copies of the CFTR gene cause thick, sticky mucus.

tossups.p: NFL quarterback Boomer Esiason started a foundation to fight this disease in 1993, after his son Gunnar was diagnosed with it. Newborn babies in the United States are screened for this disease using a few drops of blood from a heel prick.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this genetic disease that makes mucus thick and sticky and leaves sweat very salty.

tossups.p: The protein at the center of this disease belongs to the ABC transporter family, but instead of pumping molecules, it works as a channel that opens when it binds ATP. That channel lets chloride ions flow out of the cells lining the lungs.
tossups.r: That channel protein is CFTR. For 10 points, name this inherited disease that causes thick, sticky mucus.

tossups.p: Newborn screening for this disease checks a baby’s blood for high levels of trypsinogen [“trip-SIN-uh-jen”], a protein made by the pancreas. This disease is most common among people of Northern European descent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this genetic disease, caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, that clogs the lungs with mucus.

tossups.p: Old European folklore warned about babies whose foreheads tasted salty when kissed, a sign now linked to this disease. The gene behind this disease sits on chromosome 7, and its most common mutation is called F508del.
tossups.r: Each child of two carrier parents has a one-in-four chance of having it. For 10 points, name this inherited disease of thick, sticky mucus.

People with it have very salty sweat, so doctors use a sweat test to diagnose it
The CFTR protein is a channel that lets chloride ions out of cells; when it fails, mucus dries out and thickens

Most common among people of Northern European descent

Trikafta (elexacaftor, tezacaftor, and ivacaftor), approved in 2019, helps the faulty channel fold correctly and stay open
Ivacaftor (Kalydeco), approved in 2012 for the G551D mutation, was the first drug aimed at its root cause

The title of the 2019 film _Five Feet Apart_ plays on the rule that people with it stay at least six feet apart to avoid sharing germs

trap.title: The disease, not the gene
trap.body: Many clues describe the CFTR gene or its chloride channel, and some real questions ask for CFTR itself, so players mix up the gene and the disease. Two other famous recessive diseases are traps too: sickle-cell disease, which bends red blood cells, and Tay-Sachs disease, which harms nerve cells. “Fibrosis” alone is not enough, and pulmonary fibrosis is a different lung condition.
trap.fix: Listen for “this disease” versus “this gene” or “this protein.” Thick mucus, salty sweat, the pancreas, chromosome 7, and F508del mean cystic fibrosis. Red blood cells, hemoglobin, and malaria mean sickle-cell disease.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cystic fibrosis (accept CF; do not accept “CFTR”)

topics.name: Cnidarians
topics.kicker: Jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones · Animals with stinging cells
topics.dates: More than 10,000 species, mostly in the sea
topics.briefing: Cnidarians (the C is silent) are soft-bodied water animals, such as jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydras, that catch food with stinging cells. Each stinging cell holds a tiny coiled harpoon that fires faster than almost anything else in nature. They have no brain, just a net of nerves, and many switch between two body shapes: an attached polyp, like a coral, and a swimming bell called a medusa.
topics.answerHtml: Cnidarians (accept Cnidaria; prompt on coelenterates; do not accept a single member such as “jellyfish”; do not accept “ctenophores”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1962, Osamu Shimomura [“oh-SAH-moo shee-moh-MOO-rah”] isolated green fluorescent protein from the crystal jelly _Aequorea victoria_ [“ee-KWOR-ee-uh vik-TOR-ee-uh”], a member of this phylum, and he later shared a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for that work. Members of this phylum have no brain, only a simple nerve net.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of animals with stinging cells called cnidocytes, including jellyfish and corals.

tossups.p: In “The Adventure of the Lion’s Mane,” Sherlock Holmes discovers that the culprit behind a seaside mystery is a giant member of this phylum. Members of this phylum have just two true tissue layers, separated by a jelly-like layer called the mesoglea [“mez-oh-GLEE-uh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes jellyfish, sea anemones, and corals.

tossups.p: _Turritopsis dohrnii_ [“tur-ih-TOP-sis DOR-nee-eye”], nicknamed the “immortal jellyfish,” is a member of this phylum that can turn back from an adult medusa into a young polyp. Many members of this phylum begin life as a free-swimming larva called a planula [“PLAN-yoo-luh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of radially symmetric animals with stinging cells, including corals and sea anemones.

tossups.p: In the 1740s, Abraham Trembley [“trahm-BLAY”] cut apart small freshwater members of this phylum and watched each piece regrow into a whole animal. Those animals, named for a many-headed monster from Greek myth, also reproduce by budding.
tossups.r: Those animals are hydras. For 10 points, name this phylum that also includes jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones.

tossups.p: Members of one class in this phylum have 24 eyes, some with lenses, arranged in four clusters called rhopalia [“roh-PAY-lee-uh”]. That class, Cubozoa, includes the sea wasp, one of the most venomous animals on Earth.
tossups.r: That class is the box jellyfish. For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that also includes corals and sea anemones.

tossups.p: The Portuguese man o’ war belongs to this phylum, but it is actually a colony of many small, specialized animals called a siphonophore [“sy-FON-uh-for”], floating under a gas-filled sail. Most members of this phylum catch prey using stinging capsules called nematocysts, which fire harpoon-like threads.
tossups.r: Those capsules are found inside stinging cells. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes jellyfish and corals.

tossups.p: Reef-building members of this phylum get much of their food from algae called zooxanthellae [“zoh-uh-zan-THEL-ee”] living in their tissues. When the water gets too hot, those animals expel the algae and turn white, a process called bleaching.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of animals with stinging cells, whose members include the corals that build coral reefs.

tossups.p: In 2020, scientists found that _Henneguya salminicola_, a tiny parasite of salmon from this phylum, has no mitochondrial genome, so it cannot use oxygen to make energy the way other animals do. That parasite belongs to a group called myxozoans [“mik-suh-ZOH-unz”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones.

tossups.p: In 2017, scientists found that the upside-down jellyfish _Cassiopea_ [“kass-ee-OH-pee-uh”] slips into a sleep-like state at night, even though members of this phylum have no brain. Instead, members of this phylum have a simple nerve net spread through the body.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of radially symmetric animals with stinging cells, including corals and sea anemones.

tossups.p: In a process called strobilation [“stroh-bih-LAY-shun”], polyps of some members of this phylum split into a stack of tiny baby medusae called ephyrae [“EF-ih-ree”]. Many members of this phylum alternate between those two forms, with polyps reproducing asexually and medusae reproducing sexually.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes true jellyfish, hydras, and corals.

tossups.p: This phylum’s class Anthozoa includes sea anemones and corals, which live only as polyps, while its class Scyphozoa [“sy-foh-ZOH-uh”] contains the true jellyfish. Other classes in this phylum include Hydrozoa, home of the freshwater hydra, and Cubozoa, the box jellyfish.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of radially symmetric animals that catch prey with stinging cells.

tossups.p: Members of this phylum have only two true tissue layers, an outer epidermis and an inner gastrodermis, with a jelly-like layer called the mesoglea [“mez-oh-GLEE-uh”] between them. Their gastrovascular cavity has just one opening, which serves as both mouth and anus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes jellyfish and sea anemones.

tossups.p: When a tiny trigger bristle is touched, a coiled thread shoots out of a capsule in one of the fastest movements in nature, injecting venom into prey. That capsule, called a nematocyst [“neh-MAT-oh-sist”], is the key weapon of this phylum.
tossups.r: Nematocysts sit inside stinging cells called cnidocytes, which give this phylum its name. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes jellyfish and corals.

tossups.p: Clownfish live safely among the tentacles of some members of this phylum, protected by a special coat of mucus. Other members of this phylum built the Great Barrier Reef, the largest structure made by living things.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes sea anemones, corals, and jellyfish.

tossups.p: Stalked jellyfish, which belong to the class Staurozoa [“stor-oh-ZOH-uh”] in this phylum, attach themselves to seaweed with a stalk instead of swimming freely. Comb jellies look similar to members of this phylum, but they belong to a separate phylum and catch food with sticky cells instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of animals with stinging cells that includes sea anemones, corals, and true jellyfish.

clues.t: Phylum of jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydras
Catch prey with stinging cells called cnidocytes, which give the group its name (from a Greek word for “nettle”)
Radial symmetry: body parts arranged in a circle around a central mouth
Two body forms: an attached, tube-shaped polyp and a free-swimming, bell-shaped medusa
A gastrovascular cavity with just one opening, which serves as both mouth and anus
Each stinging cell holds a capsule called a nematocyst, which fires a coiled, harpoon-like thread
No brain: a simple nerve net spreads through the body
Only two true tissue layers, the epidermis and gastrodermis, with jelly-like mesoglea between them
Reef-building corals host algae called zooxanthellae; in water that is too hot, corals expel them and turn white (bleaching)
Small freshwater hydras reproduce by budding and can regrow from pieces
Clownfish live safely among sea anemone tentacles, protected by a coat of mucus
Classes include Anthozoa (corals and anemones), Scyphozoa (true jellyfish), Cubozoa (box jellyfish), and Hydrozoa
The Portuguese man o’ war is a floating colony called a siphonophore, not a single true jellyfish
Many alternate forms: polyps reproduce asexually, while medusae reproduce sexually
Osamu Shimomura found green fluorescent protein (GFP) in the crystal jelly _Aequorea victoria_ and shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
In the Sherlock Holmes story “The Adventure of the Lion’s Mane,” the culprit is a lion’s mane jellyfish, one of the largest known jellyfish
_Turritopsis dohrnii_, the “immortal jellyfish,” can turn back from an adult medusa into a young polyp
In the 1740s, Abraham Trembley showed that cut-up hydras regrow; the hydra is named for the many-headed monster of Greek myth
Box jellyfish (Cubozoa) have 24 eyes, some with lenses, in four clusters called rhopalia; the sea wasp is among the most venomous animals
Their free-swimming larva is a planula; in strobilation, some polyps split into tiny baby medusae called ephyrae
The tiny salmon parasite _Henneguya salminicola_, a myxozoan, was found in 2020 to have no mitochondrial genome
The upside-down jellyfish _Cassiopea_ slips into a sleep-like state at night even without a brain
Touching a tiny trigger bristle fires the nematocyst’s thread, one of the fastest movements in nature
Coral polyps built the Great Barrier Reef, the largest structure made by living things
Stalked jellyfish (Staurozoa) attach to seaweed with a stalk instead of swimming
Comb jellies (ctenophores) look similar but form a separate phylum and catch food with sticky cells instead of stinging cells

trap.title: Phylum, not jellyfish
trap.body: Many clues describe one famous member, like a box jellyfish’s eyes or a hydra regrowing, so players blurt “jellyfish” or “hydra,” but the question wants the whole phylum. Comb jellies (ctenophores) are the sneakiest trap: they look like jellyfish but form their own phylum, swim with rows of beating cilia, and have no stinging cells. “Coelenterates” is an older name for a group that also included comb jellies, so it earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for “this phylum” or “these animals” and answer “cnidarians” (the C is silent). Stinging cells, nematocysts, polyps and medusae, and corals mean cnidarians; rows of shimmering cilia called combs mean ctenophores.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cnidarians (accept Cnidaria; prompt on coelenterates; do not accept a single member such as “jellyfish”)

topics.name: E. coli
topics.kicker: Rod-shaped gut bacterium · Biology’s favorite lab organism
topics.briefing: E. coli, short for _Escherichia coli_, is a rod-shaped bacterium that lives by the billions in the intestines of people and other warm-blooded animals. Most kinds are harmless or even helpful, but a few strains can cause food poisoning, which is why food-safety rules call for cooking ground beef all the way through. Because it is easy to grow and can divide about every 20 minutes, it is one of the most-studied living things in science.
topics.answerHtml: E. coli (accept Escherichia coli; prompt on Escherichia or coliform bacteria; do not accept “Salmonella” or “Shigella”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1885, a German-Austrian pediatrician who was studying bacteria in infants discovered this organism, which was later renamed in his honor. This organism is Gram-negative, so it stains pink, not purple, in a Gram stain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterium that lives in the human gut and whose harmful strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: In 1988, Richard Lenski began growing twelve populations of this organism in a long-term experiment, and after tens of thousands of generations, cells in one of them evolved the ability to feed on citrate when oxygen is present. Samples frozen every 500 generations serve as that experiment’s “fossil record.”
tossups.r: This organism can divide about every 20 minutes. For 10 points, name this rod-shaped gut bacterium.

tossups.p: In 1958, Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew this organism on food containing heavy nitrogen-15 and followed its DNA through new generations, showing that DNA copies itself semiconservatively. Their experiment separated the DNA by density in a spinning centrifuge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium, a favorite model organism that lives in the human intestine.

tossups.p: In 1946, Joshua Lederberg and Edward Tatum showed that strains of this organism could swap genes, a process now called bacterial conjugation. Cells of this organism that carry the F plasmid, or fertility factor, build a bridge called a pilus to pass DNA to other cells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gut bacterium, known by a short form of its Latin name, whose dangerous strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: The restriction enzyme EcoRI, which cuts DNA wherever it finds the sequence GAATTC, takes the first part of its name from this organism. Restriction enzymes like that one help this organism defend itself by chopping up the DNA of invading viruses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium that lives in human intestines and is a favorite of biology labs.

tossups.p: In 1973, Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen made some of the first recombinant DNA by putting a plasmid carrying foreign genes into this organism. Genetically engineered strains of this organism later produced human insulin, which in 1982 became the first approved drug made with recombinant DNA.
tossups.r: This organism’s harmful strains can cause food poisoning. For 10 points, name this common gut bacterium, a favorite model organism.

tossups.p: The genome of this organism’s laboratory strain K-12, about 4.6 million base pairs long, was published in 1997 by Frederick Blattner’s team. In the human gut, this organism helps make vitamin K.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium that lives in the intestines and whose dangerous strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: A 1993 outbreak traced to undercooked hamburgers from Jack in the Box restaurants, which sickened hundreds of people, led the United States to tighten its rules on ground beef. That outbreak was caused by a strain of this organism called O157:H7, which makes Shiga toxin.
tossups.r: Most strains of this organism are harmless. For 10 points, name this bacterium that lives in the human intestine.

tossups.p: Grown on EMB, or eosin methylene blue, agar, colonies of this organism show a shiny, metallic green sheen. Water is tested for this coliform bacterium as a sign of contamination by sewage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium found in the human gut, whose harmful strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: In 1952, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase showed that DNA carries genetic information by tagging T2 phages, viruses that infect this organism, with radioactive phosphorus and sulfur. Another virus that infects this organism, lambda, can hide inside its DNA as a prophage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterium that lives in the human intestine and is a favorite model organism.

tossups.p: François Jacob and Jacques Monod [“moh-NOH”] worked out the lac operon, a set of genes for digesting the sugar lactose, by studying this organism. This organism swims with whiplike flagella in a pattern known as “run and tumble.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped gut bacterium whose dangerous strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: During World War I, Alfred Nissle isolated a strain of this organism from a soldier who stayed healthy during an outbreak of dysentery, and that strain, Nissle 1917, became a widely used probiotic. In the gut, this organism helps make vitamin K.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium whose harmful strains, such as O157:H7, can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: _Shigella_ [“shih-GEL-uh”] bacteria, which cause dysentery, are so closely related to this organism that some scientists consider them strains of it. Like _Salmonella_, this organism is a Gram-negative member of the family Enterobacteriaceae [“en-ter-oh-bak-teer-ee-AY-see-ee”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium that lives in human intestines and is a favorite lab organism.

tossups.p: This organism is a facultative anaerobe, meaning it can grow with or without oxygen, so it can live in the oxygen-poor large intestine. This organism is Gram-negative, with a thin cell wall wrapped in an outer membrane.
tossups.r: Its species name refers to the colon. For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium that lives in the guts of warm-blooded animals and is a favorite of biology labs.

tossups.p: Arthur Kornberg discovered DNA polymerase I, the first known enzyme that builds DNA, by studying extracts of this organism in 1956. Genetically engineered strains of this organism were later used to produce human insulin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gut bacterium that divides about every 20 minutes in the lab and whose harmful strains cause food poisoning.

trap.title: Not Salmonella
trap.body: E. coli and Salmonella are both rod-shaped, Gram-negative gut bacteria in the same family, and both are famous for food poisoning, so players mix them up. Shigella is even closer: it is so similar to E. coli that some scientists call it a kind of E. coli, but it is still named separately. “Coliform” is a bigger group that includes E. coli, so it earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Lab-history clues, such as Meselson and Stahl, Lederberg and Tatum, the lac operon, EcoRI, and Lenski’s experiment, point to E. coli, biology’s favorite model organism. Raw eggs, chicken, and typhoid fever point to Salmonella. Say “E. coli” or the full name, not just “coliform.”
trap.line: Real answer line: E. coli (accept Escherichia coli; prompt on Escherichia)
